claim: Frontal association cortex (FrA) pyramidal neurons of mice integrate auditory cues and basolateral amygdala (BLA) inputs non-linearly in a NMDAR-dependent manner.
source: Here, we show that frontal association cortex (FrA) pyramidal neurons of mice integrate auditory cues and basolateral amygdala (BLA) inputs non-linearly in a NMDAR-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings and optogenetic manipulations showing non-linear integration that is blocked by NMDAR antagonists.

claim: The response of FrA pyramidal neurons was more pronounced to Gaussian noise than to pure frequency tones.
source: We found that the response of FrA pyramidal neurons was more pronounced to Gaussian noise than to pure frequency tones
evidence: Demonstrated through in vivo whole-cell recordings and calcium imaging showing larger depolarizations and more dendritic events with Gaussian noise.

claim: The activation of BLA-to-FrA axons was the strongest in between conditioning pairings.
source: and that the activation of BLA-to-FrA axons was the strongest in between conditioning pairings.
evidence: Shown by two-photon calcium imaging of BLA-to-FrA axons during fear conditioning, with quantification of calcium transient frequency.

claim: Blocking BLA-to-FrA signaling specifically at the time of presentation of Gaussian noise (but not 8 kHz tone) between conditioning trials impaired the formation of auditory fear memories.
source: Blocking BLA-to-FrA signaling specifically at the time of presentation of Gaussian noise (but not 8 kHz tone) between conditioning trials impaired the formation of auditory fear memories.
evidence: Demonstrated through optogenetic inhibition experiments with ArchT during fear conditioning and subsequent behavioral testing.

claim: Discriminative learning depends on the repeated contingency and contiguity between sensory cues (conditioned stimuli, CS) and the events (e.g. danger, safety) that they must predict (unconditioned stimuli, US).
source: Discriminative learning is an important survival strategy that depends on the repeated contingency and contiguity between sensory cues (conditioned stimuli, CS) and the events (e.g. danger, safety) that they must predict (unconditioned stimuli, US) (Hall, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature on learning theory.

claim: The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) has appeared over the past decade as a critical region that shapes behaviors in response to both aversive and non-aversive environmental cues.
source: The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) has appeared over the past decade as a critical region that shapes behaviors in response to both aversive and non-aversive environmental cues (Likhtik and Paz, 2015; Likhtik et al., 2014; Stujenske et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research on mPFC function.

claim: The mPFC does not receive direct sensory information neither from sensory cortical areas or from the thalamus.
source: However, the mPFC does not receive direct sensory information neither from sensory cortical areas or from the thalamus (Hoover and Vertes, 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to anatomical connectivity study.

claim: The frontal association cortex (FrA) receives inputs from the BLA and sensory cortices.
source: Specifically, the frontal association cortex (FrA), a region of the lateral part of the agranular cortex (Paxinos and Franklin, 2001; Uylings et al., 2003), receives inputs from the BLA (Lai et al., 2012; Mátyás et al., 2014; Nakayama et al., 2015) and sensory cortices (Hoover and Vertes, 2007; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The FrA appears non-reciprocally connected to the PL/IL subdivisions of the mPFC.
source: In addition, the FrA appears non-reciprocally connected to the PL/IL subdivisions of the mPFC (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to anatomical connectivity study.

claim: The pharmacological inactivation of FrA neurons alters both the expression and extinction of learned fear.
source: For example, the pharmacological inactivation of FrA neurons alters both the expression and extinction of learned fear (Lai et al., 2012; Nakayama et al., 2015; Sacchetti et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior pharmacological studies.

claim: Fear conditioning and extinction induce dendritic spine elimination and formation in the FrA, respectively.
source: Recently, fear conditioning and extinction have been shown to induce dendritic spine elimination and formation in the FrA, respectively (Lai et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior imaging study.

claim: WGN evoked a subthreshold depolarization in naive animals that lasted for at least 30 s after the end of the stimulation.
source: WGN evoked a subthreshold depolarization in naive animals (27.6 ± 4 mV, n = 22 cells) that lasted for at least 30 s after the end of the stimulation (32.5 ± 5 mV, n = 22 cells) (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo whole-cell recordings with quantification of cumulative voltage changes, shown in Figure 1.

claim: WGN-evoked changes in membrane potential were abolished by the application of the NMDAR antagonist D(-)−2-amino-5-phosphonovaleric acid (dAP5) or the presence of the NMDAR open-channel blocker MK-801 in the intracellular solution.
source: These changes in Vm, which were always higher than those evoked by the linear chirps or the pure tones (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), were abolished by the application of the NMDAR antagonist D(-)−2-amino-5-phosphonovaleric acid (dAP5) or the presence of the NMDAR open-channel blocker MK-801 in the intracellular solution (end of the stimulation; control: 27.6 ± 4 mV, n = 22 cells; +dAP5: −13.4 ± 5 mV, n = 14 cells; +iMK801: −2.2 ± 2 mV, n = 5 cells; p<0.001, anova) (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–F)
evidence: Demonstrated by pharmacological manipulation experiments with statistical comparison.

claim: Pure auditory tones did not affect membrane potential during or after auditory stimulation.
source: In contrast, pure auditory tones did not seem to affect membrane potential either during (8 kHz: 1.2 ± 4 mV; WGN: 27.6 ± 4 mV; n = 22 cells, p<0.001, paired t-test) or after auditory stimulation (8 kHz: −3.8 ± 3 mV; WGN: 32.5 ± 5 mV; n = 22 cells, p<0.001, paired t-test).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo whole-cell recordings with statistical comparison between tone types.

claim: Pure tones affected membrane potential of FrA neurons in the presence of dAP5 or iMK801.
source: Nonetheless, we found that 8 kHz tones affected membrane potential of FrA neurons in the presence of dAP5 or iMK801 (end of stimulation; control: 1.16 ± 3.9 mV, n = 22 cells; +dAP5: −16.7 ± 4 mV, n = 10 cells; +iMK801: −21 ± 3.5 mV, n = 5 cells; p=0.004, anova) (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: Demonstrated by pharmacological experiments showing effects only when NMDARs are blocked.

claim: The NMDAR-mediated component of the evoked cVm change was much larger in response to WGN than pure auditory tones.
source: However, on average, the NMDAR-mediated component of the evoked cVm change was much larger in response to WGN, indicating that it recruited more NMDAR conductances than pure auditory tones (WGN: 33.1 ± 4.2 mV; 8 kHz: 9.7 ± 3.4 mV; n = 5 cells; p=0.017, paired t-test) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G–J).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing NMDAR-mediated components calculated from pharmacological experiments.

claim: WGN evoked significantly more local dendritic events per dendrite than pure frequency auditory tones during anesthesia.
source: The presentation of WGN evoked more events (WGN: 409; 8 kHz: 139; 2 kHz: 102; p<0.001, McNemar's χ² test), with a significantly higher number of local dendritic events per dendrite as compared to pure frequency auditory tones (WGN: 0.11 ± 0.01 Hz; 8 kHz: 0.04 ± 0.01 Hz; 2 kHz: 0.04 ± 0.007 Hz; n = 9 mice; p<0.001, anova) (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Demonstrated by two-photon calcium imaging of dendrites in anesthetized mice with statistical analysis.

claim: Eight kHz and 2 kHz tones did not evoke calcium transients more frequently than baseline during anesthesia.
source: Eight kHz and 2 kHz tones did not evoke calcium transients more frequently than baseline (Figure 2D).
evidence: Shown by comparison of event frequencies during baseline and tone presentation in calcium imaging data.

claim: WGN evoked significantly more local events per dendrite than pure tones in awake mice.
source: Again, and as expected, WGN evoked significantly more local events per dendrite than pure tones (WGN: 0.11 ± 0.01 Hz; 8 kHz: 0.08 ± 0.005 Hz; 2 kHz: 0.07 ± 0.007 Hz; n = 5 mice; p<0.001, anova) (Figure 2F)
evidence: Demonstrated by two-photon calcium imaging in awake mice with statistical comparison.

claim: Eight kHz and 2 kHz tones generated more local events in awake mice as compared to baseline.
source: Nevertheless, 8 kHz and 2 kHz tones generated more local events as compared to baseline (Figure 2F)
evidence: Shown by calcium imaging data comparing event frequencies during baseline and tone presentation in awake mice.

claim: Anesthesia might reduce dendritic signaling of pure frequency auditory inputs.
source: suggesting that anesthesia might reduce dendritic signaling of pure frequency auditory inputs (0.04 ± 0.009 Hz vs. 0.08 ± 0.05 Hz; p=0.037) (Figure 2I).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of dendritic event frequencies between anesthetized and awake conditions.

claim: The specific effect of WGN on FrA neurons was not attributable to the intensity of the tones.
source: However, the specific effect of WGN on FrA neurons was not attributable to the intensity of the tones (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: Demonstrated by testing different sound intensities and showing WGN effects persist across intensities.

claim: The specific effect of WGN on FrA neurons was not attributable to noise-induced pain since exploratory motor behaviors were not affected by WGN or pure tones.
source: or to noise-induced pain since exploratory motor behaviors were not affected by WGN or pure tones (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral analysis showing no differences in locomotor activity between tone types.

claim: Inhibiting the activity of FrA neurons during CS- presentation significantly decreased the fraction of ArchT-mice that learned the association when WGN was used as CS-.
source: In contrast, ArchT stimulation during CS- presentation (Figure 3G,H) significantly decreased the fraction of mice that were conditioned. However, this occurred only when WGN was used as CS- (protocol 1, GFP: 75%, n = 12 mice, ArchT: 30%, n = 13 mice, p=0.02; protocol 2, GFP: 85%, n = 7 mice, ArchT: 91%, n = 11 mice, p=0.7, Pearson's χ² test) (Figure 3I).
evidence: Demonstrated by optogenetic inhibition experiments during fear conditioning with behavioral testing.

claim: In mice where FrA neurons were inhibited during WGN CS-, the magnitude of CS+ evoked freezing responses was significantly lower during recall than in control mice.
source: In those mice, the magnitude of CS+ evoked freezing responses was significantly lower during recall than in control mice (protocol 1, GFP: 51 ± 7%, n = 12 mice; ArchT: 24.5 ± 5%, n = 13 mice; p=0.005) (Figure 3J).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of freezing behavior during recall after optogenetic manipulation.

claim: WGN (CS-) generated less local dendritic activation during recall as compared to naive mice.
source: As compared to naive mice, WGN (CS-) generated less local dendritic activation during recall (protocol 1; naive: 0.11 ± 0.01 Hz, n = 9 mice; FC: 0.06 ± 0.009 Hz, n = 5 mice; p=0.003) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing dendritic calcium imaging data before and after fear conditioning.

claim: Local dendritic events evoked by a conditioned cue (8 kHz) or cues that were not presented during conditioning (2 kHz) were not altered by fear learning.
source: In contrast, local dendritic events evoked by a conditioned cue (8 kHz) or cues that were not presented during conditioning (2 kHz) were not altered
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing dendritic event frequencies for different tones before and after conditioning.

claim: WGN-induced somatic plateau potentials were reduced in conditioned animals in a learning-dependent manner.
source: In addition, WGN-induced somatic plateau potentials were reduced in conditioned animals in a learning-dependent manner, suggesting that NMDAR-dependent plasticity mechanisms in FrA neurons were engaged during learning (Lai et al., 2012; Rioult-Pedotti et al., 2000; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-cell recordings after conditioning showing correlation between learning and reduced WGN responses.

claim: BLA neurons project to the superficial layer 1 of the ipsilateral FrA (<150 µm from the pia).
source: Results confirmed that BLA neurons project to the superficial layer 1 of the ipsilateral FrA (<150 µm from the pia) (Lai et al., 2012; Mátyás et al., 2014; Nakayama et al., 2015; Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Confirmed by viral tracing and imaging of BLA axons in FrA, supported by prior anatomical studies.

claim: The activity of individual BLA-to-FrA boutons increased significantly upon successive pairings only in mice that learned.
source: While the activity of individual BLA boutons in FrA was relatively low at rest, it increased significantly upon successive pairings (Figure 4D). This occurred independently of the conditioning protocol and only in mice that learned (learning+, all CS+: 1.73 ± 0.3, all CS-: 2.07 ± 0.45, n = 5 mice; learning-, all CS+: 0.62 ± 0.08, all CS-: 0.77 ± 0.13, n = 5 mice; p=0.015) (Figure 4D,E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by two-photon calcium imaging of BLA axons during conditioning with comparison between learners and non-learners.

claim: The activity of BLA-to-FrA axons never occurred before the end of the first US presentation.
source: Interestingly, it also never occurred before the end of the first US presentation.
evidence: Observed from temporal analysis of calcium transients during conditioning trials.

claim: The number of transients observed during the first CS+ (before the delivery of the first US) was significantly lower than the other CS that were paired with the US in learning mice.
source: Indeed, the number of transients observed during the first CS+ (i.e. before the delivery of the first US) was significantly lower than the other CS that were paired with the US (learning+, CS/No US: 1.03 ± 0.15, CS/US: 1.97 ± 0.4, n = 5 mice, p=0.011; learning-: CS/No US: 0.74 ± 0.05, CS/US: 0.68 ± 0.08, n = 5 mice, p=0.863) (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of calcium transients across conditioning trials.

claim: The activity of boutons measured during the first CS- was always higher than during the first CS+ in learning mice.
source: As a consequence, the activity of boutons measured during the first CS- was always higher than during the first CS+ (learning+, CS+1: 1.03 ± 0.15, CS-1: 2.03 ± 0.4, n = 5 mice, p=0.003; learning-, CS+1: 0.74 ± 0.05, CS-1: 0.88 ± 0.09, n = 5 mice, p=0.425) (arrow in Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing calcium transient frequencies between first CS+ and CS- presentations.

claim: BLA-to-FrA axons were never activated by auditory stimulations in naive mice (before fear conditioning).
source: In addition, BLA-to-FrA axons were never activated by auditory stimulations in naive mice (i.e. before fear conditioning) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by calcium imaging in naive mice showing no response to auditory tones.

claim: The averaged cumulative ΔF/F0 measured during CS- was always higher than during CS+.
source: The averaged cumulative ΔF/F0 measured during CS- was always higher than during CS+ (CS-: 0.27 ± 0.07 ΔF/F0, CS+: 0.21 ± 0.06 ΔF/F0, n = 10 mice; p=0.012)
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of cumulative calcium signals during different conditioning stimuli.

claim: The difference between CS+ and CS- related axonal activity (Δcumulative) was significantly higher in mice that learned the association than in non-learners.
source: Importantly, the difference between CS+ and CS- related axonal activity (Δcumulative: ΔF/F0 CS- - ΔF/F0 cs+) was significantly higher in mice that learned the association than in non-learners (learning+: 0.1 ± 0.02 Δcumulative, n = 5 mice; learning-: 0.01 ± 0.008 Δcumulative, n = 5 mice; p=0.013, t-test) (Figure 4F).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing differential axonal activity between learners and non-learners.

claim: The Δcumulative correlated positively with learning performance.
source: In fact, when plotted as a function of freezing percentage observed during recall, the Δcumulative correlated positively with learning performance (r²=0.89, p<0.001) (Figure 4G)
evidence: Demonstrated by correlation analysis between axonal activity measure and behavioral performance.

claim: Local photostimulation of ChR2-BLA axons in acute slices produced excitatory postsynaptic current (EPSC) in FrA pyramidal neurons with short latencies and low jitter.
source: Local photostimulation of ChR2-BLA axons in acute slices produced excitatory postsynaptic current (EPSC) in FrA pyramidal neurons with short latencies (3.5 ± 0.36 ms, n = 9 cells) and low jitter (0.289 ± 0.04 ms, n = 9 cells), suggesting that a fraction of BLA neurons are connected monosynaptically to L2/3 FrA pyramidal neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E; Klavir et al., 2017).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro slice electrophysiology with optogenetic stimulation.

claim: The photostimulation of BLA neurons with an implanted optical fiber produced plateau-like depolarizations in all FrA neurons.
source: In vivo, the photostimulation of BLA neurons with an implanted optical fiber produced plateau-like depolarizations in all FrA neurons (averaged peak amplitude: 6.2 ± 1.2 mV*sec, full-width at half-max (fwhm): 551 ± 80 ms; n = 13 cells).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo whole-cell recordings with optogenetic stimulation.

claim: BLA-to-FrA inputs were mostly undetectable and became visible only when the stimulation was delivered during down states.
source: However, BLA-to-FrA inputs were mostly undetectable and became visible only when the stimulation was delivered during down states (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G)
evidence: Demonstrated by analyzing responses during different phases of spontaneous activity.

claim: The rhythmic stimulation of ChR2-expressing BLA neurons at 0.9 Hz for 30 s generated modest cumulative depolarization.
source: The rhythmic stimulation of ChR2-expressing BLA neurons at 0.9 Hz for 30 s (27 square pulses, 50 ms) (Figure 5B,C), a protocol that mimicked the pattern of auditory stimuli, generated modest cumulative depolarization (8 ± 4 mV; n = 21 cells).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo whole-cell recordings with patterned optogenetic stimulation.

claim: The coincident photo-activation of BLA neurons during the presentation of WGN resulted in somatic responses that were significantly higher than the arithmetic sum of individual depolarizations evoked by the stimulation of BLA or auditory tones alone.
source: The coincident photo-activation of BLA neurons during the presentation of WGN did not generate somatic action potential. However, it resulted in somatic responses (observed cVm) that were significantly higher than the arithmetic sum (expected cVm) of individual depolarizations evoked by the stimulation of BLA or auditory tones alone (observed cVm: 44 ± 6.4 mV, expected cVm: 18 ± 8.8 mV, n = 11 cells; p=0.002, paired t-test) (Figure 5D,E,H; Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing observed responses to expected linear sum in paired experiments.

claim: The interaction in FrA neurons between BLA and WGN-related inputs was clearly supralinear.
source: We then plotted the observed vs. expected cVm change and found that the observed cVm exceeded the expected cVm, indicating that the interaction in FrA neurons between BLA and WGN-related inputs was clearly supralinear (Spruston and Kath, 2004; Tran-Van-Minh et al., 2015; Figure 5H).
evidence: Demonstrated by plotting observed vs. expected responses showing deviation from linearity.

claim: The application of dAP5 to the cortical surface blocked the effect of BLA activation during WGN.
source: Accordingly, we found that the application of dAP5 (1 mM) to the cortical surface blocked the effect of BLA activation during WGN (BLA+WGN: 39 ± 6.2 mV, n = 13 cells; BLA+WGN/+dAP5: −26.6 ± 6.7 mV, n = 7 cells; p<0.001; t-test), indicating that NMDARs are involved in the supra-linear integration in FrA neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Demonstrated by pharmacological blockade of NMDARs during combined stimulation.

claim: The photo-activation of BLA significantly affected the cumulative potential evoked by 8 kHz in a supra-linear manner.
source: The photo-activation of BLA also significantly affected the cumulative potential evoked by 8 kHz (8 kHz: 9.7 ± 3.3 mV vs. 8 kHz+BLA: 16.6 ± 3.1 mV; n = 8 cells; p<0.001; paired t-test) (Figure 5F,G; Figure 5—figure supplement 2D,E). Although supra-linear (observed cVm: 16.6 ± 3.1 mV, expected cVm: −2.4 ± 3.3 mV, n = 8 cells; p<0.001, paired t-test)
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing observed and expected responses for 8 kHz tone with BLA stimulation.

claim: The BLA+WGN integration was significantly stronger than the BLA+8 kHz integration.
source: the BLA+8 kHz integration remained significantly lower than the supra-linearity generated by BLA+WGN (observed cVm; WGN: 44 ± 6.4 mV, n = 11 cells; 8 kHz: 16.6 ± 3.1 mV, n = 8 cells; p=0.003, t-test).
evidence: Demonstrated by statistical comparison of non-linear integration magnitude between tone types.

claim: BLA-to-FrA neurons do not send collaterals to the prelimbic and infralimbic subdivisions of the mPFC.
source: In contrast to BLA neurons that project directly to the mPFC (Hoover and Vertes, 2007; Likhtik and Paz, 2015; Senn et al., 2014), BLA-to-FrA axons do no send collaterals to the prelimbic and infralimbic subdivisions of the mPFC (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: Demonstrated by retrograde tracing showing absence of labeled axons in mPFC subdivisions.

claim: The time-locked suppression of BLA-to-FrA communication during negatively paired WGN (CS-, protocol 1b) significantly decreased the fraction of ArchT-mice that learned the association.
source: We found that the time-locked suppression of BLA-to-FrA communication during negatively paired WGN (CS-, protocol 1b) significantly decreased the fraction of ArchT-mice that learned the association (GFP: 87.5%; ArchT: 22%, p=0.005, Pearson's χ² test) and freezing behaviors upon subsequent CS+ (8 kHz) presentation (GFP: 55.9 ± 8%, n = 8 mice; ArchT: 34.9 ± 3%, n = 7 mice; p=0.037, t-test) (Figure 6E,F; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by optogenetic inhibition of BLA-to-FrA projections during conditioning with behavioral testing.

claim: Neither the fraction of mice that learned nor freezing responses during recall were affected by blocking the activity of BLA-to-FrA axons during negatively-paired 8 kHz (CS-, protocol 2b).
source: In contrast, neither the fraction of mice that learned (GFP: 78%; ArchT: 44%, p=0.145, Pearson's χ² test) nor freezing responses during recall (CS+; GFP: 34.8 ± 3.9, n = 9 mice; ArchT: 29.3 ± 8, n = 9 mice; p=0.530, t-test) were affected by blocking the activity of BLA-to-FrA axons during negatively-paired 8 kHz (CS-, protocol 2b) (Figure 6E,G).
evidence: Demonstrated by optogenetic inhibition experiments showing no effect when 8 kHz is CS-.

claim: Fear conditioning with protocol one produced more freezing responses in control mice than with protocol 2.
source: In support of this hypothesis, fear conditioning with protocol one produced more freezing responses in control mice than with protocol 2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing behavioral outcomes between different conditioning protocols.

claim: CS+ evoked freezing responses were significantly lower during recall in mice that were conditioned in the absence of CS-.
source: In addition, CS+ evoked freezing responses were significantly lower during recall in mice that were conditioned in the absence of CS- (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing freezing responses between protocols with and without CS- presentation.

claim: The FrA may function as a relay station during learning from sensory cortical areas and the BLA to the mPFC.
source: Thus, the FrA may function as a relay station during learning from sensory cortical areas and the BLA to the mPFC.
evidence: Inferred from anatomical connectivity patterns and functional data showing FrA integrates sensory and BLA inputs.

claim: Multiple frequencies composing WGN might promote the activation of a dense pattern of neighboring spines that in turn facilitate the generation and propagation of local non-linear events toward the soma.
source: Although we cannot rule out that WGN tones are structured and further abstracted throughout the entire auditory system (Deneux et al., 2016), the simplest explanation is that frequency-tuned spines are distributed widely and heterogeneously throughout the same FrA dendrite, as already reported in the auditory cortex of anesthetized mice (Chen et al., 2011). As a consequence, the multiple frequencies composing WGN might promote the activation of a dense pattern of neighboring spines that in turn facilitate the generation and propagation of local non-linear events toward the soma (Antic et al., 2010).
evidence: Inferred from dendritic imaging data and supported by citations to prior work on dendritic spine properties.

claim: BLA-to-FrA synapses are likely to be weak and unreliable.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that BLA-to-FrA synapses are likely to be weak and unreliable.
evidence: Inferred from in vivo recordings showing modest and variable responses to BLA stimulation.

claim: BLA neurons might signal to frontal circuits any new association independently of its valence, which might subsequently be assigned by the mPFC.
source: BLA neurons might signal to frontal circuits any new association independently of its valence, which might subsequently be assigned by the mPFC (Klavir et al., 2013; Likhtik and Paz, 2015).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of BLA function based on data showing activation independent of CS type, supported by citations.

claim: Acoustic noise can enhance signal processing, facilitate sensory signaling and improve cognitive performance, notably in individuals with poor attention.
source: While acoustic noise is often viewed as a disturbing variable, it can enhance signal processing, facilitate sensory signaling and improve cognitive performance, notably in individuals with poor attention (McDonnell and Abbott, 2009; McDonnell and Ward, 2011; Stein et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on stochastic resonance and noise effects on cognition.

claim: Given that noise is abundant in the environment and communication of most mammals, it might facilitate learning in coordination with BLA-to-FrA inputs.
source: Therefore, given that noise is abundant in the environment and communication of most mammals, it might facilitate learning in coordination with BLA-to-FrA inputs.
evidence: Speculative interpretation connecting environmental noise prevalence to the observed learning facilitation mechanism.
